# Introduction

Longitudinal data, characterised by repeated measurements of the same
variables over successive time points (referred to as *waves*), are common in
medicine, economics, and the social sciences. Unlike ordinary tabular data,
they carry a temporal structure across repeated measurements of the same
covariate, and that structure is easily lost under standard preprocessing.
`scikit-longitudinal` (`Sklong`) is an open-source Python library that
addresses these challenges by providing tools for machine learning on
longitudinal data while remaining close to the familiar `scikit-learn`
ecosystem [@provost2025sklong].

This article introduces the Time-penalized Trees (TpT)
[@valla2024tpt], a recent primitive of `Sklong` that adds a new
longitudinal-data-aware decision-tree splitter to the library. It extends
standard split selection to longitudinal data by penalizing candidate splits
placed at later observation waves, allowing earlier measurements to be
preferred when impurity reduction is comparable.

Instead of reproducing the full methodological development of TpT
[@valla2024tpt], we focus on the software side of the contribution, structured
as follows. We first present the TpT split criterion in `Sklong` and briefly
recap a recent theoretical analysis showing that TpT is a consistent estimator
across a non-empty set of observation times under explicit structural
assumptions [@valla2026consistency]. Second, we describe the reproducible setup
adopted throughout the paper, including the Python environment and the
data preparation pipeline. Third, we document the TpT Application Programming
Interface (API), walking through installation, reshaping, and the main
hyperparameters. We then present two computational examples on public
longitudinal datasets, one classification and one regression, to illustrate
the splitter's behaviour. We conclude with a short discussion of the splitter's
current scope and limitations, and of directions for future work.

Tree-based methods for longitudinal or clustered data already span several
families. Model-based recursive partitioning and generalized linear model trees
target subgroup structure through parameter-instability ideas
[@zeileis2008mob; @seibold2019glmtrees]. RE-EM trees and mixed-effects random
forests incorporate random effects to account for within-subject or within-cluster
dependence [@sela2012reem; @hajjem2014merf]. Survival-tree extensions such as
LTRC trees can also accommodate time-varying covariates in censored settings
[@fu2017ltrc]. Closer to TpT, lexicographic optimisation approaches to
longitudinal decision-tree classifiers keep the standard split score and break
ties in favour of more recent features, yielding models that lean on later
waves [@ribeiro2024lexico]. TpT occupies a complementary niche: it keeps the
CART impurity objective itself and modifies the split-selection criterion
through an explicit time penalty, making the fitted tree directly readable in
terms of both predictor and wave [@valla2024tpt].

The repository is structured as required by Computo [@computo]: the paper is
written in Quarto, the environment is frozen in `environment.yml`, and the data
preparation and analysis code are kept alongside the manuscript.

# The TpT splitter in `scikit-longitudinal`

Recursive partitioning grows a tree by repeatedly splitting a parent node into
child nodes that are more homogeneous with respect to the target variable. In
other words, each split is chosen to reduce within-node heterogeneity, or
equivalently to maximize the loss of impurity from the parent node to its
children [@breiman1984cart].

For a classification node $g$, let $p_k(g)$ denote the proportion of class
$k \in \{1, \ldots, K\}$ inside the node. An impurity measure should be
nonnegative, equal to $0$ when the node is pure, maximal at the uniform class
distribution, and symmetric in the class labels. Two standard choices are the
entropy

$$
I_{\text{Ent}}(g) = -\sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k(g)\log p_k(g)
$$

and the Gini impurity

$$
I_{\text{Gini}}(g) = \sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k(g)\left(1 - p_k(g)\right)
= 1 - \sum_{k=1}^{K} p_k(g)^2.
$$

For regression, CART typically uses the node mean squared error

$$
I_{\text{MSE}}(g) = \frac{1}{N(g)}
\sum_{i: x^{(i)} \in g} \left(y^{(i)} - \bar y_g\right)^2,
$$

where $\bar y_g$ is the empirical mean response in node $g$. If a parent node
$g_p$ is split into left and right child nodes $g_l$ and $g_r$, the usual CART
goodness-of-split is the impurity decrease

$$
\Delta I(g_p; g_l, g_r) =
I(g_p) -
\left[
\frac{N(g_l)}{N(g_p)} I(g_l) +
\frac{N(g_r)}{N(g_p)} I(g_r)
\right],
$$

with $I(g)$ standing for one of the classification impurities above, or for the
MSE in regression.

At a tree node associated with parent time index $t_p$, TpT modifies this
criterion and scores a candidate split at time $t_c$ by multiplying the usual
impurity improvement $\Delta I$ by an exponential time penalty:

$$
G_{\gamma} = \Delta I \exp \left[-\gamma (t_c - t_p)\right].
$$

The hyperparameter $\gamma \ge 0$ controls how strongly later measurements are
penalized. When $\gamma = 0$, TpT reduces to ordinary impurity-based split
selection. As $\gamma$ increases, the tree becomes more reluctant to use later
waves unless they bring a clearly stronger impurity reduction.

From a user perspective, the main entry points are
`TpTDecisionTreeClassifier` and `TpTDecisionTreeRegressor`. Both estimators
operate on wide-format data together with `features_group` metadata that
encodes which columns belong to the same longitudinal feature across waves.
Long-format data must therefore be converted to wide-format beforehand, which
is handled in `Sklong` by the public `LongitudinalDataset.to_wide` API
([documentation](https://scikit-longitudinal.readthedocs.io/latest/API/data_preparation/longitudinal_dataset/);
[tutorial](https://scikit-longitudinal.readthedocs.io/latest/tutorials/long_wide_reshape/)).
We use this official reshape path in both examples below.

For this article, we select $\gamma$ on a small candidate grid
by minimizing the fitted tree's weighted total leaf impurity on the training
split. This is a pragmatic paper-specific heuristic whose only goal is to keep
the examples deterministic and easy to rerun; it should not yet be interpreted
as a recommended general tuning rule for applied work.

## A compact theoretical guarantee

TpT is not only a practical heuristic. In @valla2026consistency, the analysis
focuses on record-high times, that is, feasible times whose penalized
population envelope dominates all later competitors. The main result requires
separated penalized-envelope gaps (Assumption A1), finite-sample attainability
of the corresponding envelope peaks (Assumption A2), the TpT-$\alpha$
branch-growing rule, and the regularity and noise assumptions needed to invoke
the Klusowski-Tian oracle inequality for depth-$K$ CART estimators
[@klusowski2024cart].

::: {.theorem}
**Theorem 1 Valla and Milhaud (2026).**
Assume (A1)--(A2), the TpT-$\alpha$ growing rule, and the regularity and noise
conditions required to apply the Klusowski-Tian oracle inequality for depth-$K$
CART estimators. For every fixed record-high time $t_k$ such that the
approximation bias vanishes as $K(t_k) \to \infty$, the estimator fitted on the
realized $t_k$-subtree satisfies

$$
\mathbb{E}\!\left[\left\lVert \hat f_{t_k, K(t_k)} - f_{t_k}^{\star} \right\rVert^2_{L^2(P_{X(t_k)})}\right]
\longrightarrow 0
\qquad \text{as } n \to \infty.
$$
:::

This is intentionally narrower than a blanket consistency claim over all time
indices. The result identifies a non-empty sequence of times at which the
penalized TpT rule recovers a consistent subtree estimator. We include this
result only to summarize the current theoretical status of TpT; the paper itself
remains focused on software usage. For an implementation-focused article, the practical
takeaway is that the TpT framework underlying the splitter now has a precise
asymptotic analysis, even though the present package implementation is discussed
here from an operational rather than theorem-verification standpoint.

::: {.callout-note}
## Current scope

The present implementation is suitable for compact reproducible examples and
software-oriented demonstrations. Missing-value routing inside the Cython TpT
splitter is still treated as future work, and monotonic constraints are
explicitly disabled for TpT at the wrapper level.
:::

# Reproducible setup

The repository contains:

- `scripts/prepare_example_data.py` to download and preprocess the open
  datasets;
- `analysis/tpt_examples.py` with helper functions used by the paper;
- `environment.yml` with a frozen Python environment.

The quick-start installation shown below is the user-facing entry point. Exact
reproduction of this paper instead relies on `environment.yml`, which fixes
Python 3.11 together with `scikit-longitudinal==0.1.9` and
`scikit-lexicographical-trees==0.0.5`. The helper script
`setup-render-ci.sh` ensures that Quarto renders against the extended tree
backend required by the TpT examples.

# Install, quick start, and main parameters

The official `scikit-longitudinal` getting-started guide is intentionally
lightweight, and the same philosophy fits this article well. For a standard Python
environment, the minimal installation is:

```bash
pip install scikit-longitudinal
```

For long-format data, the recommended TpT workflow is to first reshape the data
into wide format with `LongitudinalDataset.to_wide`, then fit
`TpTDecisionTreeClassifier` (or `TpTDecisionTreeRegressor`) on the resulting
wide matrix together with its `features_group` metadata:

```{python}
#| eval: false
from scikit_longitudinal.data_preparation import LongitudinalDataset
from scikit_longitudinal.estimators.trees import TpTDecisionTreeClassifier

train_dataset = LongitudinalDataset(file_path=None, data_frame=train_long_df)
X_train = train_dataset.to_wide(
    id_col="subject_id",
    time_col="wave",
    longitudinal_columns=["marker_a", "marker_b"],
    wave_format="{feature}_t{wave}",
)
y_train = train_long_df.groupby("subject_id")["target"].first().loc[X_train.index]

test_dataset = LongitudinalDataset(file_path=None, data_frame=test_long_df)
X_test = test_dataset.to_wide(
    id_col="subject_id",
    time_col="wave",
    longitudinal_columns=["marker_a", "marker_b"],
    wave_format="{feature}_t{wave}",
)

tpt = TpTDecisionTreeClassifier(
    gamma=0.01,
    criterion="entropy",
    max_depth=2,
    min_samples_leaf=10,
    features_group=train_dataset.feature_groups(),
)

tpt.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = tpt.predict(X_test)
```

The small set of parameters that matters most in practice is summarized in
@tbl-tpt-main-parameters.

| parameter | role |
|:--|:--|
| `gamma` | Penalizes later split times when their impurity gain is similar to earlier alternatives. |
| `max_depth`, `min_samples_leaf`, `min_samples_split` | Control tree size and minimum node size. |
| `features_group` | Maps each longitudinal predictor to the columns that correspond to its observed waves. |
| `LongitudinalDataset.to_wide(...)` | Public reshape step used before fitting TpT on long-format data. |
| `wave_format` | Names the wave-expanded columns of the reshaped matrix. |
| `criterion` | Use entropy for classification and squared error (MSE) for regression. |

: Minimal set of TpT parameters most relevant for the examples in this article. {#tbl-tpt-main-parameters}

When the data are already stored in wave-separated columns, or when TpT is used
inside a broader `scikit-longitudinal` workflow, the package documentation
recommends the same building blocks as the rest of the library: a
`LongitudinalPipeline`, a time-aware preprocessing step such as
`MerWavTimePlus`, and a final estimator. A minimal pipeline skeleton is:

```{python}
#| eval: false
from scikit_longitudinal.data_preparation import MerWavTimePlus
from scikit_longitudinal.estimators.trees import TpTDecisionTreeClassifier
from scikit_longitudinal.pipeline import LongitudinalPipeline

feature_groups = [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]
non_longitudinal_features = []
feature_names = [
    "marker_a_t0", "marker_a_t1", "marker_a_t2",
    "marker_b_t0", "marker_b_t1", "marker_b_t2",
]

pipeline = LongitudinalPipeline(
    steps=[
        ("merwav", MerWavTimePlus()),
        ("tpt", TpTDecisionTreeClassifier(gamma=0.01, features_group=feature_groups)),
    ],
    features_group=feature_groups,
    non_longitudinal_features=non_longitudinal_features,
    feature_list_names=feature_names,
    update_feature_groups_callback="default",
)
```

This article keeps the examples at the estimator level, but the API is compatible
with these larger package workflows. In particular, the two examples below are
meant to bridge the package documentation and practical usage: both start from
public long-format datasets, reshape them with the official
`LongitudinalDataset` API, and then fit TpT at the estimator level.

# Data sets

The two examples use small public repeated-measures datasets with complementary
temporal structures, summarized in @tbl-dataset-summary. We cite
`scikit-longitudinal` through its JOSS software paper [@provost2025sklong].
The `pbcseq` data contain follow-up laboratory measurements for the randomized
Mayo Clinic primary biliary cirrhosis trial, with visits planned at 6 months,
1 year, and yearly thereafter [@dataset-pbcseq]. The `Produc` data form a
balanced annual panel of 48 US states from 1970 to 1986 [@dataset-produc].
Together they provide two deliberately different views of TpT: a subject-level
clinical classification problem with irregular follow-up, and a compact
multi-wave regression panel where the effect of $\gamma$ on selected split times
is easy to inspect.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-dataset-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Compact summary of the two public datasets used in the paper."
#| tbl-colwidths: [10, 14, 18, 24, 20]
from analysis.tpt_examples import dataset_summary_table

dataset_summary_table()
```

# Example 1: Subject-level classification on `pbcseq`

Our classification example uses `pbcseq`, the sequential primary biliary
cirrhosis follow-up data distributed with the `survival` package
[@dataset-pbcseq]. We keep four complete longitudinal biomarkers (`bili`,
`albumin`, `protime`, and `ast`) and define a binary target equal to one when
the subject experiences either transplantation or death by the end of
follow-up. Because the current TpT implementation operates on wide matrices and
missing-value routing is still future work, we build a dense modeling cohort by
retaining subjects with at least five recorded visits, keeping the first five
visits per subject, indexing them by visit order, and reshaping that long table
with `LongitudinalDataset.to_wide`. This yields 183 subjects and 5 visit-order
waves (@tbl-dataset-summary).

The example is run on a subject-level train/test split after reshaping. The
minimal fit/predict workflow is:

```{python}
#| eval: false
from scikit_longitudinal.data_preparation import LongitudinalDataset
from scikit_longitudinal.estimators.trees import TpTDecisionTreeClassifier

train_dataset = LongitudinalDataset(
    file_path=None,
    data_frame=train_df[["id", "visit_index", "bili", "albumin", "protime", "ast"]],
)
X_train = train_dataset.to_wide(
    id_col="id",
    time_col="visit_index",
    longitudinal_columns=["bili", "albumin", "protime", "ast"],
    wave_format="{feature}_t{wave}",
)
y_train = train_df.groupby("id")["event"].first().loc[X_train.index]

test_dataset = LongitudinalDataset(
    file_path=None,
    data_frame=test_df[["id", "visit_index", "bili", "albumin", "protime", "ast"]],
)
X_test = test_dataset.to_wide(
    id_col="id",
    time_col="visit_index",
    longitudinal_columns=["bili", "albumin", "protime", "ast"],
    wave_format="{feature}_t{wave}",
)

clf = TpTDecisionTreeClassifier(
    gamma=selected_gamma,
    criterion="entropy",
    max_depth=2,
    min_samples_leaf=10,
    random_state=42,
    features_group=train_dataset.feature_groups(),
)

clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = clf.predict(X_test)
proba = clf.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
```

The selected gamma comes from the training-grid search shown in
@tbl-pbcseq-gamma-search and visualized in @fig-pbcseq-gamma-profile.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-pbcseq-gamma-search
#| tbl-cap: "Gamma search for the pbcseq classification example. The search uses a 0.001 grid, but the table keeps only distinct training tree-total-impurity values and breaks ties by retaining the smallest gamma."
#| tbl-colwidths: [18, 28, 26, 14, 14]
pbcseq_example.gamma_table.round(4)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-pbcseq-gamma-profile
#| fig-cap: "Lower-envelope training tree-total-impurity profile for the pbcseq classification example, extracted from the full 0.001 gamma grid by keeping the local minima of the oscillating path."
#| out-width: "88%"
full_profile = pbcseq_example.gamma_profile.copy().reset_index(drop=True)
values = full_profile["tree_total_impurity"].to_numpy()
mask = [False] * len(full_profile)
for idx in range(len(full_profile)):
    left = values[idx - 1] if idx > 0 else values[idx]
    right = values[idx + 1] if idx < len(full_profile) - 1 else values[idx]
    mask[idx] = (values[idx] <= left) and (values[idx] <= right)
profile = full_profile.loc[mask].copy()
selected_gamma = pbcseq_example.metrics["selected_gamma"]
selected_row = profile.loc[profile["gamma"].eq(selected_gamma)].iloc[0]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.6, 4.1))
ax.plot(
    profile["gamma"],
    profile["tree_total_impurity"],
    color=PAPER_COLORS["teal"],
    linewidth=1.2,
    alpha=0.8,
    marker="o",
    markersize=1.8,
    markerfacecolor="white",
)
ax.axvline(selected_gamma, color=PAPER_COLORS["gold"], linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5)
ax.scatter(
    [selected_gamma],
    [selected_row["tree_total_impurity"]],
    s=70,
    color=PAPER_COLORS["gold"],
    edgecolor="white",
    linewidth=0.8,
    zorder=3,
)
ax.annotate(
    f"selected gamma = {selected_gamma:.3f}",
    xy=(selected_gamma, selected_row["tree_total_impurity"]),
    xytext=(14, 12),
    textcoords="offset points",
    color=PAPER_COLORS["ink"],
)
ax.set_xlabel("Gamma")
ax.set_ylabel("Training tree total impurity")
ax.margins(x=0.04)
plt.show()
```

The resulting subject-level metrics are shown in @tbl-pbcseq-metrics. A small
preview of the held-out predictions is given in @tbl-pbcseq-predictions.
On this dense five-visit cohort, the `max_depth=2`, `min_samples_leaf=10`
configuration selects `gamma = 0.181` and still uses later history: the
learned tree splits at visit-order waves 3 and 4 rather than collapsing to
baseline-only rules. This is precisely the behaviour we want to expose in the
article: the time penalty regularizes the use of history without erasing it
when later measurements still provide a clearly better impurity reduction.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-pbcseq-predictions
#| tbl-cap: "Preview of held-out subject-level predictions for the pbcseq classification example."
#| tbl-colwidths: [16, 24, 24, 36]
pbcseq_example.predictions.head(8).round(3)
```

The fitted tree is displayed below with the dedicated `plot_tree` exporter,
using the wide feature names built during the explicit reshape step.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\clearpage
:::

```{python}
#| label: fig-pbcseq-tree
#| fig-cap: "Selected TpT classification tree on pbcseq, displayed with the dedicated plot_tree exporter."
#| out-width: "100%"
from sklearn import tree
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 6))
tree.plot_tree(
    pbcseq_example.model,
    feature_names=pbcseq_example.feature_names,
    filled=True,
    rounded=True,
    fontsize=9,
    tpt_time_scale=0.5,
    ax=ax,
)
ax.set_title(f"TpT classification tree (selected gamma = {pbcseq_example.metrics['selected_gamma']})")
plt.show()
```

This is precisely the kind of output we want in this article: the fitted tree
shows explicitly which wave-specific biomarkers were selected by TpT, while the
calling interface remains close to ordinary `scikit-learn` usage. The node
labels make the classifier interpretable in both dimensions at once: which
biomarker matters, and at which follow-up wave it becomes decisive for the split.
In this run, the selected nonzero gamma still preserves later information:
bilirubin enters at visit-order waves 3 and 4, and albumin at wave 4.

# Example 2: State-level regression on `Produc`

Our regression example uses `Produc`, a public US state production panel
available through Rdatasets [@dataset-produc]. The source data contain
48 states followed yearly from 1970 to 1986. We keep three longitudinal
predictors available at each wave: private capital stock (`pc`), employment
(`emp`), and unemployment rate (`unemp`).
For each state, we hold out the final recorded gross state product and predict
that `final_gsp` from the preceding 16 yearly observations. We keep `Produc`
deliberately: although it is an economic panel rather than an individual-level
biomedical cohort, its 17 annual waves and three interpretable predictors make
the effect of the TpT time penalty easy to see in a small real dataset. To keep
the example readable while still producing a nonzero selected gamma and
non-baseline splits on the training impurity criterion, we use the predictor
subset `pc`, `emp`, and `unemp` together with a depth-4 tree,
`min_samples_leaf=1`, and `min_samples_split=2`.

In this example we explicitly reshape the state panel with
`LongitudinalDataset.to_wide(...)`, then fit the regressor on the resulting
wide matrix and its `features_group` metadata. The minimal workflow is:

```{python}
#| eval: false
from scikit_longitudinal.data_preparation import LongitudinalDataset
from scikit_longitudinal.estimators.trees import TpTDecisionTreeRegressor

train_dataset = LongitudinalDataset(
    file_path=None,
    data_frame=train_df[["state", "time_index", "pc", "emp", "unemp"]],
)
X_train = train_dataset.to_wide(
    id_col="state",
    time_col="time_index",
    longitudinal_columns=["pc", "emp", "unemp"],
    wave_format="{feature}_t{wave}",
)
y_train = train_df.groupby("state")["final_gsp"].first().loc[X_train.index]

reg = TpTDecisionTreeRegressor(
    gamma=selected_gamma,
    criterion="squared_error",
    max_depth=4,
    min_samples_leaf=1,
    min_samples_split=2,
    random_state=42,
    features_group=train_dataset.feature_groups(),
)

reg.fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = reg.predict(X_test)
```

selected_gamma = produc_example.metrics["selected_gamma"]
selected_row = profile.loc[profile["gamma"].eq(selected_gamma)].iloc[0]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(7.1, 6.4), sharex=True, height_ratios=[3, 2])

ax = axes[0]
ax.plot(
    profile["gamma"],
    profile["tree_total_impurity"],
    color=PAPER_COLORS["coral"],
    linewidth=2.3,
    marker="o",
    markersize=4.5,
    markerfacecolor="white",
)
ax.axvline(selected_gamma, color=PAPER_COLORS["gold"], linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5)
ax.scatter(
    [selected_gamma],
    [selected_row["tree_total_impurity"]],
    s=70,
    color=PAPER_COLORS["gold"],
    edgecolor="white",
    linewidth=0.8,
    zorder=3,
)
ax.annotate(
    f"selected gamma = {selected_gamma:.3f}",
    xy=(selected_gamma, selected_row["tree_total_impurity"]),
    xytext=(14, 12),
    textcoords="offset points",
    color=PAPER_COLORS["ink"],
)
ax.set_xlabel("Gamma")
ax.set_ylabel("Training tree total impurity")
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(billion_formatter)
ax.margins(x=0.04)

ax2 = axes[1]
ax2.plot(
    profile["gamma"],
    profile["root_time"],
    color=PAPER_COLORS["ink"],
    linewidth=2.0,
    marker="o",
    markersize=4,
    label="root time",
)
ax2.plot(
    profile["gamma"],
    profile["min_split_time"],
    color=PAPER_COLORS["teal"],
    linewidth=1.8,
    marker="s",
    markersize=3.8,
    label="min split time",
)
ax2.plot(
    profile["gamma"],
    profile["max_split_time"],
    color=PAPER_COLORS["plum"],
    linewidth=1.8,
    marker="^",
    markersize=4,
    label="max split time",
)
ax2.axvline(selected_gamma, color=PAPER_COLORS["gold"], linestyle="--", linewidth=1.5)
ax2.set_xlabel("Gamma")
ax2.set_ylabel("Selected split time")
ax2.legend(frameon=False, loc="upper right", ncol=3)
ax2.margins(x=0.04)
plt.show()
```

```

The selected regression tree can also be shown directly with the dedicated
`plot_tree` exporter.

On the article grid from `0.000` to `0.100` by `0.001`, the selected
regression gamma is `0.011`. The corresponding tree still uses later history,
with selected split times between waves 1 and 5. As gamma increases further on
that grid, the tree is pulled back toward baseline: the root split moves to
wave 0 by about `gamma = 0.031`, and from about `gamma = 0.055` onward all
selected split times are at baseline. The gamma path therefore shows the
intended TpT tradeoff quite clearly: modest penalization still allows
mid-history splits when they materially reduce impurity, whereas stronger
penalization progressively collapses the tree toward earlier waves.

```{python}
#| label: fig-produc-tree
#| fig-cap: "Selected TpT regression tree on Produc, displayed with the dedicated plot_tree exporter."
#| out-width: "100%"
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 6.6))
tree.plot_tree(
    produc_example.model,
    feature_names=produc_example.feature_names,
    filled=True,
    rounded=True,
    fontsize=7,
    tpt_time_scale=0.18,
    ax=ax,
)
ax.set_title(f"TpT regression tree (selected gamma = {produc_example.metrics['selected_gamma']})")
plt.show()
```

This makes the regression example a useful complement to `pbcseq`: the exported
tree tells us not only which economic predictor matters, but also whether it
matters near the beginning of the panel or later in the observed trajectory. In
the selected tree, the root decision already depends on employment at wave 1,
while deeper refinements still use later information through private capital at
wave 2 and employment again at wave 5.

# Discussion

These two examples are intentionally small. Their role is not to provide a full
benchmarking study, but to document a reproducible and inspectable usage path
for TpT within `scikit-longitudinal`. Together they show that public long-format
data can be reshaped through the official `LongitudinalDataset` API, tuned with
a simple deterministic gamma heuristic for demonstration purposes, and exported
as readable wave-indexed trees.

Most importantly for this article, the exported trees show both what matters and
when it matters. In `pbcseq`, the classifier can isolate clinically meaningful
biomarker thresholds at specific follow-up waves rather than collapsing the
history into a single summary. In `Produc`, the regression tree reveals whether
private capital, employment, or unemployment becomes informative early or later
in the state-level trajectory. This predictor-plus-wave readability is the main
practical property we wanted to make visible.

The paper also has clear limits. We deliberately keep the methodological
discussion short, we do not attempt a large comparative benchmark, and the
gamma-selection rule used here is only a reproducible placeholder rather than a
definitive model-selection recommendation. On the software side, missing-value
routing inside the Cython TpT splitter is still future work.

Natural next steps are equally clear: implement survival-specific evaluation
metrics, add richer visualization utilities such as subject-level trajectory
displays inside the fitted tree, build ensemble methods on top of the current
splitter, and generalize the time penalty so that prior temporal structure such
as lagged predictor effects can be encoded directly. Because TpT is now
integrated into the tree-building backend, these extensions are largely a
question of design and validation rather than reimplementing the core split rule
from scratch.

Within that scope, TpT already has the ingredients of a useful
`scikit-longitudinal` contribution: a lightweight API, interpretable exported
trees, and a growing theoretical foundation.
